Breadboard test

Wire the clock's electronics up on a breadboard and check every part works, before you solder anything or print the case. You add one part at a time and test it, so if something doesn't work you know exactly where to look. No soldering is needed except for the parts that only come with solder pads (the USB-C breakout, the LED and the ring). Allow an evening.

Where does the ESP32 go?

Pick one; the pictures and wire lists below change to match. Your ticks are kept separately for each.

Before you start

How a breadboard works

Three kinds of jumper wire

With the ESP32 plugged in, a wire to one of its pins goes into a free hole in the same row of five as that pin, so those ends are male. Modules have pins, so their end of a wire is female.

The ESP32 sits next to the breadboard and you connect to its pins with the female end of a jumper. Most modules have pins too, so a female–female jumper goes straight from the ESP32 to the module.

Wire colours used here

3.3 V5 Vground (GND)signals

Your jumpers can be any colour, but sticking to red for 5 V, orange (or another one colour) for 3.3 V and black for ground makes mistakes easy to spot.

⚠️ Golden rules. Unplug the USB cable (and later the 5 V adapter) every time you change wires. Keep the ESP32 on your computer's USB the whole time and never connect the 5 V adapter to its 5V pin. Make sure the two ground rails stay joined.

You'll also want the two small 6 × 6 mm push buttons from your tactile switch kit; the 16 mm panel buttons need soldering, so they go in during final assembly.

1

Flash the firmware

⏱ 10 min

No wiring yet. Get the ESP32 running first, on its own, so you know the board and the firmware are good before anything else is connected.

You need: ESP32-S3 boardUSB-C data cableComputer
  1. Plug the USB-C cable into the port marked USB on the ESP32 (the board has two; this one carries the log).
  2. Flash the firmware from the Firmware page: the web flasher needs nothing installed.
  3. Open a serial monitor at 115200 baud (the web flasher has one, or PlatformIO's monitor).
  4. On your phone, join the Wi-Fi network CeilingClock-Setup and pick your home network.
✅ Test it: Open http://ceilingclock.local/ on your phone or computer. You should see the clock's page with the time and a green synced just now.
Not working?
ceilingclock.local doesn't open
Some Android phones don't support .local names. Use the IP address printed in the serial monitor instead.
Nothing in the serial monitor
Use the port marked USB, not UART, at 115200 baud. Some USB-C cables only carry power: try another.
No CeilingClock-Setup network
Press the RST button on the ESP32 and wait 20 seconds.
2

ESP32 onto the breadboards, and power rails

⏱ 10 min

The ESP32 is too wide for one breadboard: on one board its pins would cover every free hole. Two boards side by side give each row of pins its own board, with free holes beside every pin. Then three short wires set up the rails: the top rails become 3.3 V and ground, the bottom rails ground for the 5 V supply.

You need: 2 full-size breadboards (830 holes)3 jumper wires: 3 male–male
⚠️ Leave the row of the ESP32's 5V pin (row 25, lower board) empty.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

  1. Unplug the USB cable.
  2. Pull the power-rail strip off one long side of one breadboard (it slides or peels off), and push that side against the other board. One rail strip is left between the two boards; the ESP32 will sit over it.
  3. Line the ESP32 up with its antenna on the left. Put the pins along its top edge into column i of the upper board and the pins along its bottom edge into column b of the lower board, with the first pins in row 5. Press down evenly on both rows of pins, not on the metal can.
  4. If the pins don't line up with columns i and b on your boards, use whichever columns fit. What matters is that each pin has free holes beside it on the outside. The free holes in the same row of five as a pin are connected to that pin.

Connect

✅ Test it: Plug the USB cable back in: the clock starts as before. With a multimeter, the top + and − rails read about 3.3 V.
Not working?
The ESP32 doesn't start on the breadboard
A pin may be folded under the board. Lift it out gently, straighten the pin and press it in again.
The ESP32 goes dark when you add the wires
The orange wire is in a ground row or rail. It must start in the row of the first pin (3V3) and end in the top + rail.
3

Buttons

⏱ 10 min

For testing, use two small 4-legged push buttons; the 16 mm panel buttons go in later. Each one sits across the gap in the middle of the breadboard. Wire to diagonally opposite legs: that way it works whichever way round the button sits. On the lower board the rows beside the ESP32 are taken, so the buttons go at the two ends.

You need: 2 small 6 × 6 mm push buttons (from your tactile switch kit)4 jumper wires: 4 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: On the clock's page, press button B: the Front display button on the page flips between on and off. Hold B for 3 seconds: Projector flips. (Button A snoozes an alarm; you'll try it later.)
Not working?
Nothing happens
Check the wires go to diagonally opposite legs (a1 and j3, a28 and j30) and that the button straddles the gap.
It acts as if always pressed
The button is turned so both wires land on legs that are always connected. Turn it 90°.
4

Front display (TM1637)

⏱ 5 min

The four-digit display that shows the time on the front of the clock. Its two data pins go straight to the ESP32; power comes from the top rails.

You need: TM1637 display4 jumper wires: 4 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The display shows the time within a second. On the settings page, change the front display's brightness: it follows.
Not working?
Display stays blank
CLK and DIO swapped? VCC must go to the + rail (3.3 V).
Shows 88:88 or garbage
A loose jumper: push each one firmly onto its pin.
5

Projector LCD (Nokia 5110)

⏱ 10 min

The LCD makes the image on the ceiling. Test it as it comes, before cutting its window: lighting its own backlight lets you read it on the bench.

You need: Nokia 5110 LCD (no need to cut it yet)8 jumper wires: 8 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The LCD shows the time, back to front: the clock mirrors it for the projector. Untick Mirror left/right in the projector settings to read it, and tick it again before testing the optics.
Not working?
Blank or solid black
Adjust LCD contrast on the settings page. Check RST and CE.
No backlight
On some boards BL lights when connected to + instead of −. Move that one wire to the top + rail.
6

Light sensor

⏱ 5 min

A light-dependent resistor and a fixed 10 kΩ resistor make a divider: the voltage between them rises as the room gets brighter. Neither part has a polarity. They go on the upper board, next to the 3.3 V rail.

You need: GL5528 light sensor10 kΩ resistor (brown-black-orange)2 jumper wires: 2 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: In the night settings, watch sensor now next to "Dark below". It goes up with a torch on the sensor and down when you cover it with a finger.
Not working?
Always about 0
The sensor leg isn't in row 13 or the orange wire isn't on the + rail.
Always about 4095
The 10 kΩ resistor isn't reaching the − rail.
7

Clock module (DS3231)

⏱ 5 min

The battery-backed clock that keeps time when Wi-Fi or power drops. Its two data pins are on the ESP32's top edge (pins 1 and 2), so these two wires start on the upper board.

You need: DS3231 module (with its coin cell)4 jumper wires: 4 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: The page shows RTC backup ok. Turn your router's Wi-Fi off and press RST on the ESP32: the time is still right.
Not working?
Still says "no RTC"
SDA and SCL swapped, or VCC on 5 V instead of 3.3 V.
ZS-042 (larger) board
It charges its battery. With a non-rechargeable CR2032, remove the 200 Ω resistor or diode beside the holder first.
8

5 V supply

⏱ 10 min

From here on, parts need more current than the ESP32 can give. The 5 V supply feeds the bottom rails only. The ESP32 stays on your computer's USB, and the grounds are already joined.

You need: USB-C breakout + 5 V 3 A adapter2 wires soldered to VBUS and GND (or header pins)
⚠️ Never connect this 5 V to the ESP32's 5V pin while the computer is plugged in: two supplies would fight through the board. In the finished clock the computer stays unplugged.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Plug the adapter in. Everything carries on as before. With a multimeter, the bottom rails read about 5 V.
Not working?
Reads 0 V
Some breakouts only switch on with a USB-C to USB-C charger and 5.1 kΩ CC resistors (yours has them). Try another cable.
9

Amplifier and speaker

⏱ 10 min

Plays the alarm sounds. The capacitor steadies its supply; the long leg is +, and the stripe marks −.

You need: MAX98357A amplifier40 mm speaker100 µF capacitor5 jumper wires: 5 female–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Screw the speaker leads into the amp's + and − terminals. Under Sounds, press Play on beep.wav: four beeps. Then give an alarm a radio or podcast URL and press Preview stream.
Not working?
Silent
Is the 5 V adapter plugged in? Check BCLK, LRC and DIN aren't swapped. Leave GAIN and SD unconnected.
Crackles
Push the capacitor's legs fully into the rails (long leg to +).
10

Sunrise ring

⏱ 10 min

The sunrise light. The 330 Ω resistor protects the ring's data input; the big capacitor smooths the current the LEDs draw. Mind the capacitor's stripe: it goes to −.

You need: WS2812B 16-LED ring (with leads soldered on)330 Ω resistor (orange-orange-brown)1000 µF capacitor4 jumper wires: 3 female–male, 1 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Give an alarm a sunrise time (for example 15 minutes) and press Ring now: the ring glows warm white until you press Dismiss (or hold button A for 2 seconds).
Not working?
Nothing lights
Make sure the wire goes to DI (in), not DO (out). Check the 5 V adapter is on.
Flickers or wrong colours
Keep the data wire short. If it persists, a 74AHCT125 level shifter on the data line fixes it.
11

Projector LED

⏱ 15 min

The bright LED that lights the LCD. The MOSFET module switches and dims it for the ESP32. The 4.7 Ω resistor limits the current to about 400 mA, and it gets warm, so keep it off the plastic.

You need: MOSFET module3 W LED on its star (leads soldered on)4.7 Ω 2 W resistorSomething metal to sit the LED on2 jumper wires: 2 female–male
⚠️ Don't look straight into the lit LED. Without its heatsink it heats up in seconds: sit the star on metal and don't leave it at full brightness for more than a few seconds.

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: On the clock's page, switch the Projector off and on: the LED goes off and on. Change the projector's day brightness: it dims.
Not working?
LED never lights
LED + and − swapped? Check OUT+ goes through the resistor to LED +.
Always on full
TRIG is on the wrong pin, or the module's trigger GND isn't connected.

2

Power rails

⏱ 5 min

The two rails along the top of the breadboard become 3.3 V (from the ESP32) and ground. Every small module will plug into them. A wire over the right-hand end joins the top ground rail to the bottom one.

You need: Breadboard3 jumper wires: 2 female–male, 1 male–male

New wires are bright and numbered; earlier ones are faded. Hover a wire in the list to find it in the picture.

Connect

✅ Test it: Nothing to see yet. If you have a multimeter, the top + and − rails should read about 3.3 V with the USB cable plugged in.
Not working?
The ESP32 goes dark or resets when you plug in the wire
The 3V3 wire is in the − rail or touching G. Unplug USB and check: orange to +, black to −.

★

Bonus: see it on the ceiling

⏱ 15 min

Once the LCD has its window cut (assembly step 5), you can try the projector by hand in a dark room before printing anything.

  1. Point the LED up, sitting on its metal.
  2. Hold a piece of baking paper about 10 mm above it, and the LCD, glass up, about 30 mm above it.
  3. Hold the lens about 106 mm above the LCD, look at the ceiling, and move the lens up and down until the digits are sharp. That's what the focus ring does in the finished clock.
  4. Use Mirror left/right and Flip projection on the clock's page until it reads right from where you lie. In the clock the mirror adds one more flip, so expect to change Mirror left/right once it's built.

Done?

When every step passes, move the same connections onto the perfboard (assembly step 4). Two things change in the finished clock: the 16 mm buttons replace the small ones, and the 5 V supply also feeds the ESP32's 5V pin, so from then on leave the computer unplugged and update the firmware over Wi-Fi. The full pin list is on the wiring page.
